newsitem.title: USA: Simpson defense rests, plaintiffs go on attack.
newsitem.headline: Simpson defense rests, plaintiffs go on attack.

text.p: The defence in O.J. Simpson's civil trial rested on Tuesday, and the plaintiffs began calling rebuttal witnesses, including a photographer who took shots of Simpson apparently wearing special designer shoes.

E.J. Flammer, a freelance photographer, testified that before a September 26, 1993, Buffalo Bills football game he took 30 photos of Simpson with a group of five men. Plaintiffs' attorneys contend that the shoes he was wearing were the expensive designer Italian shoes Bruno Magli.

FBI shoeprint expert William Bodziak testified earlier that size 12 Bruno Maglis with a distinctive sole pattern left a trail of bloody prints from the where Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman were stabbed to death on June 12, 1994.

Simpson, who was acquitted in October 1995 of the murders of his ex-wife and her friend and now faces a wrongful-death civil suit brought by the victims' families, has denied ever owning a pair of Bruno Maglis. He wears size 12 shoes.

Flammer, 24, said he made six colour prints for the men in the picture with Simpson and one black and white photograph. The negatives remained in his darkroom until Dec. 27 1996, when he hired an agent and a lawyer, he added.
Simpson's defence has tried to prove that another photograph of Simpson, taken at the same game by a different photographer, Harry Scull, had been doctored.
The defence testimony came earlier from Robert Groden, a photographic laboratory technician who said there were several problems with Scull's photo.

But FBI photo expert Gerald Richards testified in rebuttal on Tuesday that one of the alterations perceived by Groden was a natural phenomenon so common in film developing that "most first-year photo students would know immediately what it was."
"There is no doubt in my mind regarding the shoes in this particular photograph that (they) have not been altered or changed in any way," Richards said.

The last witness for the defence was the ex-football star's eldest daughter, Arnelle, who testified that her father was "shocked, very upset, sad, confused" when he learned of his ex-wife's death by telephone in his Chicago hotel room.
Arnelle Simpson, 28, said she was awakened by two detectives at about 5:30 a.m. on the day after the murders.
She said she took the detectives to the main section of her father's mansion and then went to her car to get the telephone number of Simpson's personal secretary who knew where he was.

"When I was going out to the car I asked them 'Please tell me what's going on, please tell me what's happened. At that point (Det. Philip Vannatter) said that Nicole ... had been killed at her house and that there was someone else with her," Arnelle Simpson said.
Asked how she reacted to the news she she replied, "I was shocked, I was stunned, upset, confused and scared."

She said she spoke to her father in Chicago by telephone. "He kept saying 'What's going on, what's going on?' and all I could tell him was Nicole's dead and there's somebody else with her," Arnelle Simpson said. "He was shocked, very upset, sad, confused."
